ABSTRACT Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) effectively mitigates the knowledge cutoff and hallucination issues of large language models by incorporating external knowledge bases. However, standard RAG applies a uniform retrieval strategy to all question types and feeds redundant retrieval results directly into the generator, leading to high token consumption and potentially degraded answer quality. This paper proposes SAC-RAG (Semantic Adaptive Compress RAG), a unified framework that integrates questiontype-adaptive retrieval with context compression. SAC-RAG first classifies queries into three types—factual, definitional, and reasoning—via an LLM classifier, applies a differentiated retrieval strategy for each type, then uses a unified LLM context compression module to extract evidence snippets, and finally generates answers from the compressed and refined context. To independently quantify the contribution of each component, we design four progressive ablation experiments on three multi-hop QA datasets—HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and MuSiQue—and evaluate using four metrics: Exact Match, F1, Recall@10, and token consumption. Experimental results show that SAC-RAG reduces token consumption by 38%–58% at the cost of only a 1–2 percentage point EM drop, with EM actually improving after compression for reasoning-type questions, achieving the optimal quality–efficiency trade-off in terms of token consumption, with a moderate increase in per-query latency due to additional LLM calls. SAC-RAG offers a modular and interpretable optimization solution for the efficient deployment of RAG in real-world settings. On the compression side, methods such as LLMLingua [5] and LongLLMLingua compress retrieved context on top of standard retrieval, effectively reducing token consumption; however, they operate on a fixed retrieval pipeline without considering question-type differences in the retrieval stage. To the best of our knowledge, no prior work unifies question-type-adaptive retrieval and context compression within a single framework. To address these limitations, this paper proposes SAC-RAG (Semantic Adaptive Compress RAG), a unified framework that integrates question-type-adaptive retrieval with context compression. SAC-RAG first classifies each user query into one of three semantic types via an LLM classifier: Fact, Definition, and Reasoning. SAC-RAG employs a differentiated retrieval strategy for each type. Fact-type questions use hybrid retrieval combining BM25 sparse retrieval and Milvus dense vector retrieval with BGE cross-encoder reranking. Definition-type questions adopt pure semantic vector retrieval. Reasoning-type questions are decomposed into multiple sub-questions by an LLM, with results merged after parallel retrieval. Once retrieval is complete, results of all types pass through a unified LLM context compression module to extract evidence snippets, which are then fed into the generator to produce the final answer. To systematically validate the independent contribution of each component, we design four progressive ablation settings on three multi-hop question answering datasets—HotpotQA [6], 2WikiMultiHopQA [7], and MuSiQue [8]—namely Naive RAG (baseline), Compress RAG (compression only), Adaptive RAG (adaptive retrieval only), and SAC-RAG (the full framework). Evaluation covers four metrics: Exact Match (EM), F1, Recall@10, and average token consumption. Experimental results show that: (1) adaptive retrieval is the primary driver of answer quality improvement, boosting EM from 0.560 to 0.611 ( +9.1%) and Recall@10 from 0.787 to 0.880 (+11.8%) on HotpotQA; (2) context compression reduces token consumption by 55–58% with EM decreasing by only 1–2 percentage points; (3) SAC-RAG achieves the optimal quality–efficiency trade-off; on Reasoning-type questions, EM improves after compression (HotpotQA: 0.455→0.577). Unlike previous studies that optimize either retrieval or compression independently, SAC-RAG coordinates semantic-aware retrieval and context compression within a unified framework. The main contributions of this paper are as follows: • A question-semantic-type-based adaptive retrieval framework with three differentiated retrieval strategies; • A unified architecture, SAC-RAG, that integrates adaptive retrieval and context compression; • Systematic ablation experiments that independently quantify the contribution of each component, providing clear guidance for RAG system optimization. EVOLUTION OF RETRIEVAL-AUGMENTED GENERATION Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) was introduced by Lewis et al. [9] in 2020, with the core idea of retrieving relevant documents from external knowledge bases as additional context before an LLM generates an answer, thereby addressing knowledge cutoff and hallucination. Early RAG systems relied on dense vector retrieval [10], mapping queries and documents into a shared vector space for nearest neighbor search. Gao et al. [11] categorized the evolution of RAG into three stages: Naive RAG uses a fixed retrieve-thengenerate pipeline; Advanced RAG introduces pre- and postretrieval optimizations such as query rewriting, reranking, and compression; Modular RAG decomposes the system into independently replaceable functional modules, supporting iterative retrieval and adaptive scheduling. A recent systematic review [12] further confirms this taxonomy through a PRISMA-compliant analysis of 128 highly cited RAG studies, identifying modular and policy-driven architectures as the prevailing trend. Within this framework, training paradigms such as Atlas [13], context-prefix schemes such as In-Context RALM [14], and standardized benchmarks such as BEIR [15] emerged in succession. As retrieved documents grow longer, however, LLMs become less effective at using key information in extended contexts [1]: redundant content not only raises computational cost but also introduces noise that can degrade answer quality. These issues are particularly acute in multi-hop reasoning, where retrieval spans multiple documents of uneven relevance, demanding both precision in retrieval strategies and efficiency in context utilization— as well as coordination between the two. Existing work addressing these bottlenecks falls into three main directions: adaptive retrieval, context compression, and joint optimization of retrieval and reasoning. B. ADAPTIVE RETRIEVAL METHODS Adaptive retrieval adjusts retrieval strategies based on query characteristics to obtain more precise context. For strategy selection, Adaptive-RAG [3] routes questions among no-retrieval, single-step, and multi-step retrieval paths based on question complexity; Self-RAG [16] uses a selfreflection mechanism to trigger retrieval on demand during generation; FLARE [17] actively supplements retrieval based on token confidence during decoding. For retrieval quality, V endi-RAG [18] introduces a diversity metric to balance coverage and relevance of retrieved documents; REPLUG [19] improves reliability through multi-retriever ensembling. On the input side, Ma et al. [20] proposed the Rewrite-Retrieve-Read framework, training a compact rewriting model to optimize queries before retrieval. More recently, LLM-based generation-augmented rewriting methods such as GaQR [21] further leverage chain-of-thought reasoning to expand queries, achieving substantial retrieval recall improvements. However, these routing methods primarily address model selection or query-complexity-based dispatch, whereas SAC-RAG adapts retrieval strategies within a unified pipeline according to semantic question types—a distinction that yields finergrained control over the retrieval process. A shared limitation of these methods is that their adaptation axis centers on question complexity or token confidence, without designing differentiated retrieval mechanisms based on question semantic type (factual, definitional, reasoning). As a result, retrieval strategies lack a structured understanding of the nature of the question. C. CONTEXT COMPRESSION METHODS Context compression aims to reduce redundancy in retrieval results, lowering token consumption during generation. LLMLingua [5] introduced selective compression of retrieval results using a small language model; LongLLMLingua [24] extended this to long-context settings. In terms of compression strategy, RECOMP [25] formalized compression as a summarization task; BRIEF [26] introduced a queryaware mechanism that doubles the compression rate while maintaining answer quality; LLMLingua-2 [27] proposed a task-agnostic data distillation approach. SARA [28] further combines fine-grained textual spans with compact semantic compression vectors to improve context efficiency under strict token budgets. The growing focus on token efficiency has also motivated agentic frameworks such as TeaRAG[29], which jointly compresses retrieved content and reasoning chains to achieve significant token reduction while preserving accuracy. A common limitation of these methods is that compression operates on top of a fixed retrieval strategy: the retrieval stage is unaware of downstream compression needs, and the compression stage does not exploit type information from the retrieval stage. The two components remain independent, lacking co-design. D. JOINT RETRIEVAL AND REASONING In multi-hop QA, retrieval and reasoning are not independent stages—reasoning requires multiple retrieval steps to supply intermediate evidence, and retrieval strategies shift dynamically with each reasoning step. Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting [30] established the approach of improving reasoning through intermediate steps; ReAct [31] interleaves reasoning and action, deciding after each reasoning step whether new retrieval is needed; IRCoT [32] embeds retrieval within each step of the CoT reasoning chain. For task decomposition, DecomP [33] and DSP [34] adopt a decompose-retrieve-merge strategy; ChainRAG [2] addresses the information loss problem in sub-question decomposition through progressive retrieval-and-rewriting over a sentence graph. KiRAG[4] further incorporates knowledge triples into iterative retrieval, bridging information gaps across reasoning steps. These works show the value of jointly optimizing retrieval and reasoning. However, they focus on retrieval–reasoning synergy, while the joint optimization of retrieval and compression remains an open problem: no existing method unifies adaptive retrieval and context compression within a single framework. RESEARCH GAP AND MOTIVATION The analysis of the three directions above reveals a shared limitation: the components of a RAG system— retrieval, compression, and reasoning—are still optimized as independent modules. Adaptive retrieval addresses how to retrieve, but does not consider how the retrieval results will be compressed; context compression addresses how to condense, but does not exploit type information from the retrieval stage to guide compression strategy; joint retrieval and reasoning demonstrates the value of co-design, but this principle has yet to be extended to retrieval and compression. The core motivation of SAC-RAG is to fill this gap: to build a unified framework in which question-type-adaptive retrieval and context compression work together. In SAC-RAG, the classifier’s output determines the retrieval strategy; the resulting type-specific retrieval outputs naturally differ in document count, redundancy, and information density, which shapes the input to the downstream compression module. Although compression itself uses a unified prompt and logic across all question types, the diversity of its inputs produces type-adaptive compression effects. This indirect coordination through the data flow distinguishes SAC-RAG from prior modular designs where retrieval and compression operate as independently configurable modules. Retrieval strategies are differentiated by semantic type, compression processes diverse retrieval outputs with a consistent logic, and the two components achieve positive complementarity in the quality–efficiency trade-off. ANAL YSIS OF COMPRESSION EFFECTS BY QUESTION TYPE The ablation results above validate the overall effectiveness of adaptive retrieval and context compression. However, a deeper question constitutes the theoretical premise of SAC-RAG’s design—does context compression affect different question types uniformly? If compression effects were type-independent, there would be no need for differentiated retrieval after classification; conversely, if different types respond to compression in significantly different ways, this validates the design rationale of ‘‘classify first, then retrieve’’ in SAC-RAG. To answer this question, Table 6 presents the percategory performance of Adaptive RAG and SAC-RAG across different question types. Reasoning questions represent the category where compression is most effective. On HotpotQA, SAC-RAG achieves an EM of 0.577 on Reasoning questions, a 26.8% improvement over Adaptive RAG’s 0.455. On 2Wiki, Adaptive RAG’s EM on Reasoning questions is as high as 0.859, while SAC-RAG achieves 0.855, essentially on par, with token consumption dropping from 3,255 to 1,490 (−54.2%). For questions involving multi-step reasoning chains, compression effectively filters out noise in the retrieved results, allowing the LLM to focus on critical evidence. On MuSiQue, the Reasoning EM decreases modestly from 0.253 to 0.220 (−3.3 pp), suggesting that when retrieval quality is already low (Recall@10=0.372–0.385), the compressed context may lose critical evidence fragments that are too sparse to survive filtering. A significant shift in the study of facial emotion recognition (FER) is observed from traditional machine learning methods to modern techniques using deep learning. The first studies allowed people to find faces, extract their features and group them. Datasets such as FER2013, CK+, JAFFE and AffectNet provided a benchmark for structured evaluations in controlled and real-world environments. Deep learning makes it easier for VGG, ResNet and convolutional neural networks to present and classify features. To make systems more robust and to cope with ambiguous labels, data-centric methods such as data augmentation and label distribution learning are proposed. However, there are still several challenges to overcome, including sensitivity to illumination and pose variations, class imbalance, annotation noise, and poor generalization to real-world scenarios. Existing models also have limited capacity in detecting subtle emotion and are not fair among diverse demographic groups. These limitations point to the need for more robust, scalable and interpretable FER systems which can operate reliably in unconstrained settings, motivating the approach proposed in this work. Lowe, Member, IEEE Abstract—For many computer vision and machine learning problems, large training sets are key for good performance. However, the most computationally expensive part of many computer vision and machine learning algorithms consists of finding nearest neighbor matches to high dimensional vectors that represent the training data. We propose new algorithms for approximate nearest neighbor matching and evaluate and compare them with previous algorithms. For matching high dimensional features, we find two algorithms to be the most efficient: the randomized k-d forest and a new algorithm proposed in this paper, the priority search k-means tree. We also propose a new algorithm for matching binary features by searching multiple hierarchical clustering trees and show it outperforms methods typically used in the literature. We show that the optimal nearest neighbor algorithm and its parameters depend on the data set characteristics and describe an automated configuration procedure for finding the best algorithm to search a particular data set. In order to scale to very large data sets that would otherwise not fit in the memory of a single machine, we propose a distributed nearest neighbor matching framework that can be used with any of the algorithms described in the paper. All this research has been released as an open source library called fast library for approximate nearest neighbors (FLANN), which has been incorporated into OpenCV and is now one of the most popular libraries for nearest neighbor matching. After evaluating many different algorithms for approximate nearest neighbor search on data sets with a wide range of dimensionality [14], [47], we have found that one of two algorithms gave the best performance: the priority search k-means tree or the multiple randomized k-d trees. These algorithms are described in the remainder of this section. 3.1. The Randomized k-d Tree Algorithm The randomized k-d tree algorithm [13], is an approximate nearest neighbor search algorithm that builds multiple randomized k-d trees which are searched in parallel. The trees are built in a similar manner to the classic k-d tree [9], [10], with the difference that where the classic kd-tree algorithm splits data on the dimension with the highest variance, for the randomized k-d trees the split dimension is chosen randomly from the top Np dimensions with the highest variance. We used the fixed value Np = 5 in our implementation, as this performs well across all our data sets and does not benefit significantly from further tuning. When searching the randomized k-d forest, a single priority queue is maintained across all the randomized trees. The priority queue is ordered by increasing distance to the decision boundary of each branch in the queue, so the search will explore first the closest leaves from all the trees. Once a data point has been examined (compared to the query point) inside a tree, it is marked in order to not be reexamined in another tree. The degree of approximation is determined by the maximum number of leaves to be visited (across all trees), returning the best nearest neighbor candidates found up to that point. Considering a node v with n, associated data points, and assuming a maximum number of iterations J in the k-means clustering loop, the complexity of the clustering operation is O(n,dK1), where d represents the data dimensionality. Taking into account all the inner nodes ona level, we have }> n, = n, so the complexity of constructing a level in the tree is O(ndK1). Assuming a balanced tree, the height of the tree will be (log n/log K), resulting in a total tree construction cost of O(ndKI(log n/log K)). Search time complexity. In case of the time constrained approximate nearest neighbor search, the algorithm stops after examining L data points. Considering a complete priority search kmeans tree with branching factor K, the number of top down tree traversals required is L/K (each leaf node contains K points in a complete k-means tree). During each top-down traversal, the algorithm needs to check O(log n/log K) inner nodes and one leaf node. For each internal node, the algorithm has to find the branch closest to the query point, so it needs to compute the distances to all the cluster centres of the child nodes, an O(Kd) operation. The unexplored branches are added to a priority queue, which can be accomplished in O(K) amortized cost when using binomial heaps. For the leaf node the distance between the query and all the points in the leaf needs to be computed which takes O( Kd) time. In summary the overall search cost is O(Ld(log n/log K)). 3.3 The Hierarchical Clustering Tree Matching binary features is of increasing interest in the computer vision community with many binary visual descriptors being recently proposed: BRIEF [49], ORB [50], BRISK [51]. Scaling to such large data sets is a difficult task, one of the main challenges being the impossibility of loading the data into the main memory of a single machine. For example, the size of the raw tiny images data set of [7] is about 240 GB, which is greater than what can be found on most computers at present. Fitting the data in memory is even more problematic for data sets of the size of those used in [4], [8], [55]. In FLANN we used the approach of performing distributed nearest neighbor search across multiple machines. 5.1 Searching on a Compute Cluster In order to scale to very large data sets, we use the approach of distributing the data to multiple machines in a compute cluster and perform the nearest neighbor search using all the machines in parallel. The data is distributed equally between the machines, such that for a cluster of N machines each of them will only have to index and search 1/N of the whole data set (although the ratios can be changed to have more data on some machines than others). The final result of the nearest neighbor search is obtained by merging the partial results from all the machines in the cluster once they have completed the search. In order to distribute the nearest neighbor matching on a compute cluster we implemented a Map-Reduce like algorithm using the message passing interface (MPI) specification. Algorithm 4 describes the procedure for building a distributed nearest neighbor matching index. Each process in the cluster executes in parallel and reads from a distributed filesystem a fraction of the data set. All processes build the nearest neighbor search index in parallel using their respective data set fractions. Test Research Paper: IoT-Based Smart Irrigation Purpose This synthetic test paper describes an IoT smart irrigation prototype. It is designed for testing document upload, retrieval, citations, and multi-document comparison. System Design The prototype uses a soil-moisture sensor, an ESP32 microcontroller, a relay module, and a water pump. The sensor is sampled every 30 seconds. When soil moisture falls below 35 percent, the controller switches the pump on. The pump switches off when moisture reaches 55 percent. This hysteresis band helps reduce rapid switching. Connectivity and Data The ESP32 sends timestamped moisture readings and pump states to a local dashboard over Wi-Fi using HTTP. If Wi-Fi is unavailable, local threshold-based operation continues and up to 500 readings are stored in a circular buffer. Evaluation Plan A proposed seven-day test compares water use against a fixed-timer irrigation baseline. Metrics include total water consumed, time below the 35 percent moisture threshold, pump activation count, and missing sensor readings. No measured experimental results are claimed. Limitations The prototype has not been field-validated. Sensor calibration may vary with soil type, salinity, and placement. The HTTP dashboard is intended for a trusted local network and does not define production-grade authentication. Quick Facts Controller: ESP32. Sampling interval: 30 seconds. Pump ON threshold: below 35 percent. Pump OFF threshold: 55 percent. Offline buffer: 500 readings. Proposed evaluation duration: seven days.

UNKNOWN: An Evidence-Grounded Hybrid Retrieval and Reasoning System for Intelligent Information Discovery Abstract—Researchers must find relevant papers, judge whether the available evidence is sufficient, detect disagreement among sources, and check their own documents against the current literature. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems usually return one fused answer and leave these judgments to the reader. This paper presents UNKNOWN, a multi-source scholarly retrieval system in which an evidence-sufficiency signal controls retrieval and answer generation. A query is decomposed into sub-questions; each is scored for sufficiency, and insufficient ones are reformulated, searched in additional sources, or reported as gaps. Every atomic claim in a generated answer, including numbers, dates and named entities, is checked against its cited passage and repaired or removed. INTRODUCTION Research relies on reading many papers. The answer to a literature question is rarely contained in one snippet: a definition may come from one paper, a number from another and a limitation from a third, and the papers may disagree. A system must therefore decide whether it has enough evidence and whether that evidence can be trusted before it answers. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) reduces unsupported answers by conditioning a language model on retrieved passages [1]. Four problems remain. First, an answer is generated even when the retrieved evidence is weak or irrelevant [2]. Second, a generated sentence may contain a number, date or name that is absent from the cited passage. Third, when papers disagree, the answer tends to blend the conflicting statements. Fourth, a user’s own document is not systematically checked against the literature. Lexical ranking with BM25 and dense retrieval over a FAISS index are standard and complementary [3]–[8]. UNKNOWN uses them as a base and does not claim them as a contribution. The contribution is the control layer around retrieval and generation: 1. Sufficiency-controlled retrieval. Evidence sufficiency is computed per sub-question across independent sources and decides whether to answer, search again, or report a gap. 2. Claim-level verification with repair. Atomic claims, including numbers, dates and names, are checked against the cited passage and corrected or removed. 3. Conflict-aware, reliability-weighted evidence. Sources are weighted by venue, recency and retraction status; disagreements are reported with both sides and a likely cause. 4. Document-versus-literature comparison. Statements in a user’s document are compared with external literature to expose outdated or contradicted claims. A typed research-gap report and evidence-linked visual tools (concept map, Knowledge DNA, 3D orbit view) are supporting features described in Section IV but not evaluated as core contributions. II. RELATED WORK A. Retrieval and Adaptive Retrieval BM25 ranks passages by term frequency, inverse document frequency and length normalization [6]. Dense retrievers compare embeddings and match paraphrases [4], [5], and FAISS supports efficient nearest-neighbor search [7]. Reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) merges ranked lists without requiring comparable scores [8], and the behavior of fusion functions has been analyzed in detail [9]. Hybrid RAG with re-ranking has also been studied in an IEEE conference paper [10], and a survey covers RAG extensions [11]. Self-RAG, CRAG and Adaptive-RAG adapt when and how to retrieve by critiquing retrieved passages or by selecting a strategy from question complexity [12]–[14]. Work on sufficient context reports that language models frequently answer even when the provided context is insufficient [2]. These works show that multi-round and adaptive retrieval is established. They do not compute sufficiency per sub-question over independent scholarly sources, nor connect that measurement to a gap report. B. Scholarly Question Answering PaperQA2 and OpenScholar answer scientific questions with citations to papers [15], [16]; Elicit and Consensus are commercial tools for literature search and synthesis [17], [18]. Knowledge-graph methods can structure extracted knowledge for LLMs [19]. In the sources we reviewed, these systems do not compare a user’s own document with the literature or repair individual claims. C. Claim Verification and Conflicting Evidence Attribution studies ask whether generated text is supported by its sources [20]. FEVER and SciFact formalize claim verification against evidence [21], [22], and ALCE and FActScore evaluate citation quality and atomic factual precision [23], [24]. VeriCite applies natural language inference to improve citations in RAG [25], and a fake-news framework retrieves external evidence to verify extracted claims [26]. Surveys explain why generated text drifts from sources [27]. Numeric and date verification inside scholarly answers has received less attention. D. Entailment and number matching can fail on paraphrase and implicit claims, and the cited passage itself may be wrong. Reliability weights. Venue and recency are imperfect proxies for quality, and retraction metadata may be incomplete; weights need tuning and bias checks. Comparison and gaps. Aligning a statement with the literature can misjudge scope, and an inferred gap needs expert confirmation. Model confidence is not a calibrated probability. Extraction. A supported node is not necessarily a correct extraction. Data and models. Only open-access text and abstracts are used, so coverage is partial; language-model output is not fully deterministic; any model-based judge can be biased; and the evaluated domains may not represent all fields. Scope. The typed gap report and the visual tools were not evaluated quantitatively. IX. UNKNOWN: An Evidence Grounded Hybrid Retrieval and Reasoning System for Intelligent Information Discovery I. Abstract Researchers must locate relevant papers, judge whether the retrieved evidence is enough, notice when sources disagree, and check their own documents against the literature; retrieval-augmented systems usually return one fused answer and leave these judgments to the reader. This paper presents UNKNOWN, a multi-source scholarly retrieval system in which an evidence-sufficiency signal controls retrieval and answer generation. Each sub-question is scored for sufficiency, and a failure triggers query reformulation, source expansion or an explicit gap report. Every atomic claim, including its numbers, dates and names, is checked against its cited passage and repaired or removed. Sources are weighted by venue, recency and retraction status, disagreements are reported together with their likely cause, and the user's own document is compared with the open literature. Research gaps are reported in three typed categories, and the overview, Knowledge DNA, mind map and 3D concept orbit show only content backed by a linked source passage. Retrieval combines BM25 and FAISS with reciprocal rank fusion inside per-user isolated workspaces, and a single deterministic confidence score is computed in the backend. The prototype is built with Python, FastAPI and Streamlit and passes 304 backend tests. The effect of the new stages has not yet been measured; the paper specifies the baselines, public benchmarks, ablations and user study that will test it. Keywords— Evidence sufficiency, retrieval-augmented generation, claim verification, conflict-aware retrieval, document-versus-literature comparison, research-gap analysis, scholarly question answering, confidence calibration. II. Introduction Research is based on reading multiple articles. Answers to a literature query are rarely confined to one snippet since an answer might require definitions from different documents, numbers from other papers, and limitations from yet another article, and all those papers might contradict each other. Thus, document retrieval alone is not sufficient since the reader has to determine whether there is enough evidence to provide an answer and whether it is credible. Scholarly search engines index papers at very large scale and rank them with text-match, citation and recency signals, but their output is a list of papers that the reader must still open, read and reconcile. Free catalogues such as OpenAlex [1] and the Semantic Scholar platform [2] now expose metadata, abstracts and citation links through public interfaces, so an answering layer can be built on open data. What such a layer still lacks is not access to papers but a disciplined way to decide when the retrieved evidence is enough, which statements it really supports, and where it disagrees with the reader's own document. Sufficiency is calculated for each sub-question across independent sources and leads to deciding to answer, re-search or report a gap, so abstention becomes a retrieval indicator, not a late decision. 2. Claim-level verification with repair. Atomic claims, consisting of numbers, dates and names, are compared against the cited passage and corrected or deleted. 3. Conflict-aware, reliability-weighed evidence. Sources are weighed based on their venue, recency and retraction status; citation count is only a weak signal. Disagreements are provided with both parties and reasons for it. 4. Document vs world comparison. The answer compares the user’s document with the web and literature, stating the agreements and discrepancies, which helps identify outdated and false claims. 5. Three-type report of research gap. III. Literature Review A. Retrieval and adaptive retrieval BM25 retrieves passages based on term frequency, inverse document frequency and normalization [7]. Dense retrievers compare passage embeddings and match paraphrases [5], [6]; FAISS enables efficient nearest-neighbours searching [8]. Rank fusion combines the ranked lists without needing compatible scores [9]. Retrieval-augmented generation was originally proposed for knowledge-rich language understanding tasks [3], and a survey discusses its extensions [10]. A cross-encoder re-ranker, which reads the query and the passage jointly, can refine the top candidates [11]; UNKNOWN treats it as an optional stage that is tested in the ablations. Self-RAG, CRAG, and Adaptive-RAG adapt when and how to retrieve by critiquing retrieved passages or selecting retrieval strategies by question difficulty [12]–[14]. STEEL, a fake news detection system, re-retrieves when first retrieved evidence is insufficient [15]. These works demonstrate that multiple rounds of retrieval have been done before. The works did not evaluate evidence sufficiency per sub-question from independent scholarly sources, nor did they relate the sufficiency measurement to a gap report. B. Scholarly question answering PaperQA2 and OpenScholar provide scientific answers using references to papers [16], [17]. Elicit and Consensus are tools for searching and synthesizing literature. Open infrastructure such as OpenAlex [1] and the Semantic Scholar Open Data Platform [2] supplies the metadata, abstracts and citation links on which such tools depend; UNKNOWN reads from these sources through a unified chunk schema (Section V-K). IV. Problem Formulation and Objectives A. Problem statement Let D = {d1, ..., dN} be a collection of academic papers which can include the user’s personal documents and other freely available documents. For a query q, the system should give back the answer a, the collection of sub-queries verdicts and the collection of differences/conflicts and gaps in the form of a report such that all the assertions made in the output are justified by the relevant document or else removed. The query q is broken down into sub-queries q1, ..., qm. The evidence Ei is returned by the retriever for each subquery qi and the sufficiency test gives any of the following three statuses – sufficient, weak and insufficient. B. Research questions RQ1. Is answer accuracy higher and are there less unsupported claims in sufficiency-controlled retrieval compared to single-pass retrieval using the same base retriever? RQ2. How accurate is the claim-level verification in identifying unsupported claims, and how many are fixed or dropped? RQ3. If there are conflicting papers, is reliability weighting presented for both sides together with the rationale? RQ4. How many out-of-date or wrong seeded statements in a user document does the document versus literature comparison reveal? RQ5. Are the limitations stated, implicit gaps and future directions identified properly and are the gap statuses correct? RQ6. Illustrative walk-through (design example, not a measured result) To show how the stages interact, consider the query “What are the limitations of BERT-style models for long documents?”. The query is decomposed into three sub-questions: the input-length limit, the computational cost, and the proposed remedies. Suppose several independent open-access papers address the length limit and the remedies, so those two sub-questions are marked sufficient, whereas only one source addresses cost, so that sub-question is marked weak. The loop then reformulates the cost query and widens the set of sources; if the status is still weak after the allowed rounds, cost is reported under “What I could not find” instead of being answered from model memory. During verification, a claim that states a token limit is kept only if that number appears in its cited passage, and an unsupported claim is repaired or dropped. The final report lists the claim labels, any conflict between sources, the confidence score with its breakdown, and the remaining gap. D. Discussion Cost is introduced by the architecture. IX. Limitations and Threats to Validity Evidence. The novelty assertion rests on searches that were not exhaustive, and the surveyed papers were assessed from abstracts and the text available to us; they should be read in full, and the search repeated immediately before submission, because this field changes quickly. Verification. Entailment and number verification may be erroneous when dealing with paraphrasing or implicit claims, and the selected passage may be erroneous. Reliability weights. Venue and recency are imperfect surrogates for quality, and retraction information could be incomplete. The weights require tweaking and testing for any bias. Comparison and gaps. Matching a statement in a document against the literature could incorrectly assess scope, while an inferred gap should be confirmed by an expert. A confidence value produced by the model cannot be interpreted as a calibrated probability. The deterministic confidence score is reproducible, but it is not a probability until it has been calibrated on held-out data and its expected calibration error has been reported. Extraction. An asserted node does not automatically mean that it is a correct extraction. Rule-based querying could misclassify a question of ambiguous intent. Data coverage. Only open-access full text and abstracts are used and paywalled papers are never scraped, so some answers rest on abstracts alone. Coverage is far smaller than that of commercial indexes, and results depend on the availability, rate limits and licences of external interfaces. Model dependence. Generation and claim verification depend on the chosen language model and entailment model, whose behaviour can change between versions; each run should therefore record the model versions used. Isolation. Namespace isolation protects stored data inside the application. It does not replace operating-system or network security, and any external language-model provider still receives the retrieved text sent to it. X. Conclusion and Future Work UNKNOWN is a scholarly information retrieval system that uses an evidence-sufficiency signal to control both retrieval and generation, verifies each claim against its cited passage, weights sources by reliability, reports conflicts and differences between a user’s document and the literature, and types and links research gaps to their evidence. It keeps each user’s documents in isolated, deletable workspaces and reports one deterministic confidence score with its breakdown. The retrieval corpus and the hybrid retriever are conventional; the contribution is the control and verification logic around them and its integration into one workflow. UNKNOWN: An Evidence Grounded Hybrid Retrieval and Reasoning System for Intelligent Information Discovery I. Abstract It is up to researchers to find relevant papers, evaluate the sufficiency of evidence, detect inconsistencies among sources, and identify discrepancies between their documents and existing literature. Retrieval-augmented approaches typically provide one fused answer and leave these judgments up to the user. This paper introduces UNKNOWN, a multi-source scholarly retrieval system wherein evidence sufficiency is responsible for retrieval and answer generation. Each sub-question is evaluated on evidence sufficiency; in case of failure, a new formulation of the question or detection of a gap is generated. Every atomic claim, such as numbers, dates and names, is verified and corrected or deleted. The sources are weighted based on venue, recency, and retractions, and disagreement is detected and reasoned. The answer highlights discrepancies between the user's document and the current literature. Research gaps are defined in three categories and presented with evidence-relevant visualization tools using only the linked source passages. The retrieval mechanism is a hybrid of BM25 and FAISS with reciprocal rank fusion, written in Python, FastAPI and Streamlit; 304 backend tests are passed. The impact of the new stages has yet to be determined; the ablation experiments and baselines are defined in the paper. Keywords— Evidence sufficiency, retrieval-augmented generation, claim verification, conflict-aware retrieval, document-versus-literature comparison, research-gap analysis, scholarly question answering. II. Introduction Research is based on reading multiple articles. Answers to a literature query are rarely confined to one snippet since an answer might require definitions from different documents, numbers from other papers, and limitations from yet another article, and all those papers might contradict each other. Thus, document retrieval alone is not sufficient since the reader has to determine whether there is enough evidence to provide an answer and whether it is credible. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) eliminates unfounded answers by providing a language model with retrieved passages [1]. Yet, existing RAG systems fail to solve the following four problems. First, an answer is generated out of the retrieved document regardless of how little or irrelevant this document is. Second, a generated sentence might mention a number, date or person which is not included in the retrieved passage. Third, when papers contradict each other, an answer tends to be an amalgamation of two contradicting facts. Fourth, if a user uploads his/her own document, the system fails to check it systematically against other literature. BM25-based lexical ranking and sentence embedding-based dense retrieval with the FAISS index are baseline methods, and both have examples that the other method can miss [2], [3], [4]. We employ them as the retrieval component without claiming them as a novel contribution. Our novel contribution is the control mechanism around the retrieval and generation processes. Contributions include: 1. Retrieval controlled by evidence sufficiency. Sufficiency is calculated for each sub-question across independent sources and leads to deciding to answer, re-search or report a gap, so abstention becomes a retrieval indicator, not a late decision. 2. Relevance and support for claims annotations will be done manually and cross-verified with another person, and the differences will be settled. Another set of questions and a set of papers with outdated information seed will be created for RQ3 and RQ4 respectively. B. Baselines and ablations In all configurations, the exact same corpus, chunking method, embedding model, and number of candidates are used. These include: BM25 [5] alone; FAISS [6] alone; hybrid search; hybrid search with complete UNKNOWN pipeline; and the complete pipeline with removal of one step at a time (sufficiency loop, claims verification, reliability, document versus world evaluation, evidence linking filtering). The direct comparison with a generic assistant (such as GPT or Claude) on the same documents needs to be done since for some documents, such an assistant will be able to answer just as well. C. Metrics Retrieval is evaluated using Recall@K, MRR, and NDCG@K. Answer quality is evaluated through the accuracy and the rate of unsupported claims. Verification is evaluated using claim-support precision and unsupported claim removal rate. Conflict detection and resolution is evaluated based on the presentation of both parties in the disagreement set. Document comparison is evaluated through the number of outdated seeded claims detected. Gap report is evaluated through the accuracy and the agreement among experts. Concept and relation extraction is evaluated through precision, recall and F1 score, and also node and edge correctness is separately evaluated. The novelty assertion is based on searches which were not exhaustive, and the ten selected papers were evaluated using abstracts and the text that is available, and they should be read completely before submission. Venue and recency are imperfect surrogates for quality, and retraction information could be incomplete. The weights require tweaking and testing for any bias. Comparison and gaps. Matching a statement in a document against the literature could incorrectly assess scope, while an inferred gap should be confirmed by an expert. A confidence value produced by the model cannot be interpreted as a calibrated probability. Extraction. An asserted node does not automatically mean that it is a correct extraction.
